# Tools: restriction enzymes, vectors, competent host

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Tools** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Biotechnology — Principles and Processes fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Tools: restriction enzymes
### vectors
### competent host

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Genetic engineering needs a standard toolkit. **Restriction enzymes** — the molecular scissors — recognise specific palindromic sequences and cut, leaving sticky or blunt ends. **Vectors** — plasmids, phage, cosmids — carry the gene into cells and replicate there; they need an origin of replication, a selectable marker and cloning sites. The **competent host** (usually *E. coli*) is made permeable so it can take up the recombinant DNA.

**Concept flow — the toolkit in working order (study in this order)**

| Step | Tool | Job |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Restriction enzyme (e.g. EcoRI) | Cuts source DNA and vector at the same recognition site |
| 2 | DNA ligase | Seals insert into vector |
| 3 | Vector (plasmid pBR322, phage lambda) | Replicates inside the host; carries selectable marker |
| 4 | Competent host (E. coli) | Takes up the recombinant DNA and expresses it |
| 5 | Selectable marker | Antibiotic resistance lets only transformed cells survive |

**Restriction enzymes — naming, recognition and cut types**

| Feature | Detail | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Naming | First letter = genus, next two = species, then strain/number | EcoRI = E. coli R strain, enzyme I |
| Recognition site | Palindromic sequence, 4–8 bp | EcoRI: GAATTC; BamHI: GGATCC |
| Sticky ends | Staggered cut leaves single-stranded overhangs | EcoRI cuts G^AATTC — the classic exam enzyme |
| Blunt ends | Straight cut across both strands | SmaI: CCC^GGG |
| Why 'restriction' | Bacteria use them to restrict invading phage DNA; they protect their own DNA by methylation | Part of the bacterial immune system |

**Vectors — requirements and types**

| Feature / type | What it provides | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Origin of replication (ori) | The vector copies itself inside the host | Every plasmid has one; copy number varies |
| Selectable marker | Distinguishes transformed cells (antibiotic resistance) | ampR, tetR genes on pBR322 |
| Cloning sites (MCS) | Recognised cutting sites for inserting the gene | Cluster of restriction sites |
| Plasmid | Small circular DNA; workhorse of cloning | pBR322, pUC |
| Phage lambda | Infects bacteria efficiently; carries larger inserts | Lambda derivatives |
| Cosmid / BAC / YAC | Carries very large DNA fragments | Used in genome projects |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — reading a plasmid map.** pBR322 carries ampR and tetR. The gene is inserted at a site inside tetR. Cells grown on ampicillin survive if they carry any plasmid; cells grown on tetracycline die if the insert disrupted tetR. So the clone of interest is: ampicillin-resistant AND tetracycline-sensitive. This is **insertional inactivation** — using the disruption of a marker gene as the selection signal.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Restriction enzymes: cut palindromic sites; EcoRI = E. coli restriction I; produce sticky ends (5' overhangs) — the nomenclature and sticky ends are the marks.
Trick 2: Vector requirements: origin of replication (ori), selectable marker (antibiotic resistance), cloning site (MCS), small size, high copy number — five criteria.
Trick 3: Competent host: CaCl2 + cold shock (0 °C → 42 °C) makes E. coli take up plasmids; alternatives: microinjection, gene gun (biolistics), electroporation — the methods list.
Trick 4: Insertional inactivation: insert in lacZ/blue-white screening — the selection trick worth a mark.
